Paleomagnetic Results
Two magnetic components were isolated in
most of the specimens for both the Lockhart
and Kawagarh formations. A low-temperature
component (LTC) was eliminated by ∼110–200
°C or ∼4–10 mT. The LTC from all the sec-
tions yields an in situ mean direction close to
the present geomagnetic field (PGF: declina-
tion (D) = 3.10°, inclination (I) = 55.5° for the
Hazara region). This suggests that the LTC is G H
of viscous origin and is not considered further
(Fig. S1; Table S3; see footnote 1). A high-tem-
perature component (HTC) was isolated be-
tween ∼200 and 550 °C or ∼12–90 mT (Fig. 5).

Therefore, they argued that this equatorial pa-
leolatitude shows a Cretaceous position for the
KLA, not for the Karakoram Block. The KLA’s
equatorial position is further confirmed by West-
erweel et al. (2019), who studied the Burma Ter-
rane, which was part of the eastern TTSS, and
concluded that it was located at a near-equatorial
southern latitude at ca. 95 Ma. Recently, Mar-
tin et al. (2020) studied the Khardung volcanics
from the Ladakh arc and found magnetite and
hematite-related primary remanence. They in-
ferred that the KLA was positioned at a paleo-
latitude of 8.1°N ± 5.6° during 61.64–66.1 Ma.
Based on the paleomagnetic results mentioned
above, it has been concluded that the KLA was
positioned at equatorial to low northern latitude
at ca. 95 Ma. Later on, it drifted northward and
reached a paleolatitude of 8.1°N ± 5.6° during
61.64–66.1 Ma.
Paleoposition of the Southernmost Margin
of Asia
Now we discuss the paleolatitude of the
southern margin of the Asia Plate. In the
study area, the southern margin of the Asia
Plate comprises the Karakoram Block, which
is sutured with the KLA by the MKT or the
Shyok-Tsangpo Suture (Fig. 1A). After the
Jurassic period, the Lhasa Block is considered
to be equivalent to the Karakoram Block, and Figure 10. Paleopoles of Cretaceous and Paleogene for the Lhasa Block. Small-circle fit-
